Putting it in the same set of materials as the write trial once led people to believe that "the old entry point is indeed unavailable" was sufficient to justify changing the request format; that inference no longer applies.

Likewise, `raw_response` is an observation point on the response-object side that still needs to be retained. It can help confirm that the response was not replaced with another object, but it cannot prove whether the request included a type when it was sent. If the trial is declared successful solely because the response field is still readable, the boundary between configuration and writing is blurred again.

The record for this round did not require all instance paths to switch immediately. A failure should also state whether it stopped during retrieval, naming, or after request formation, rather than recording only an exception name.

If neither of these two conditions is met, that only means this instance sample did not expose a problem; it does not mean queries, imports, or other model paths can be changed along with it.

# Mongoid Import Options History

The ordering of import options was initially treated as a small compatibility issue: callers had already supplied options, batch import would also add its own options, and the verification environment required no stale caches or personal configuration. The initial draft focused on "who overrides whom" and used the adapter file as the starting point for investigation. Later review did not establish that implementation belonged at this starting point, so the initial draft's limitation is retained rather than being recast as an apparently stable Mongoid rule.

## Scope Captured at the Time

The first option was to derive the merge order directly from `elasticsearch-model/lib/elasticsearch/model/adapters/active_record.rb`. It was not adopted. This path was indeed an entry point left by the earlier investigation, suitable for checking local declarations in existing Ruby modules and adjacent call names; however, Active Record in the path name cannot prove that Mongoid import options are implemented there. Treating it as the sole source would cause later readers to misread a navigation relationship as an implementation relationship.

The second option was to define a fixed precedence first and then use the check results to fill in the rationale. It was not adopted either. At the time, there was no evidence covering all caller combinations, only one clean-environment check requirement: record whether the import took the creation path or the no-creation path. It could help rule out local-state interference, but it could not replace a judgment about the override order.

The decision that remains is narrow: continue to treat ordering as a problem of combining caller options with batch-import options; have check records describe only the creation or no-creation path actually observed; and require any change that would state the ordering as a compatibility commitment to return to the actual place where that combination is handled. This decision allows pre-release checks to continue, but does not assign ownership to the implementation layer.

This scope also determines how the review notes are written. The creation path and no-creation path are outcomes that may be recorded during checks, not labels for option ordering. Even if two checks observe the same path, that can only indicate that the environment in that run was not altered by stale caches or personal configuration; it cannot answer whether a caller-supplied value takes effect before or after the options added by the batch.

## Legacy Judgments Retained from the Initial Draft

The initial draft said, "The order should be handled where caller options are merged." That statement remains useful because it prevents batch-processing behavior from being misattributed to index lifecycle or relationship scopes; it is not, however, a confirmed call chain. Later review only confirmed that the adapter path remains usable for checking historical behavior; it did not establish that Mongoid options enter that path, leave it, or are rewritten by a preprocessing step.

Accordingly, the original "Keeping the existing checks is sufficient" also needs to be read in its original context. It referred to the release check at the time; it does not mean that the current import interface has an established order for every option combination. That judgment remains here because it explains why the issue was not escalated to an adapter change.

There was also discussion at the time of writing "batch options take precedence" into the release notes, on the grounds that the batch side was closer to the import operation; that rationale did not become a decision. Instead, hard-coding precedence up front would silently override existing caller configuration before it had been checked case by case, and would cause people troubleshooting issues later to treat the release notes as a fact about the code. Deferring it was not because ordering was unimportant, but because the only things that could be confirmed at the time were the check environment and path records; the combination point itself was missing from the evidence.

## Two Questions Separated During Review

During review, someone raised import ordering alongside other compatibility items. The field name exposed by the response object remains `raw_response`; this is part of the result object's interface contract and does not indicate the override direction for Mongoid import options. The boundary of another old entry point was also handled separately: loading the removed `Elasticsearch::Persistence::Model` persistence mode must raise `LoadError`, and that constant must not be defined. This describes load behavior after the entry point was removed; likewise, it cannot establish how batch-import options are merged.

title: Hit Order Adjustment Proposal

versions.body:
# Hit Order Adjustment Proposal

This interface review focuses on where record ordering comes from in ActiveRecord relation queries. Search already supplies the hit order, but the relation may still arrange records by its own rules when the caller has not specified a sort order; as a result, once the same batch of hits reaches the page, the order users see no longer matches the search results. Compatibility work for 2026.7 should address this gap only in the default branch, rather than introducing a separate sorting mechanism for all relation queries.

The proposed rule is: when the caller has not specified an explicit sort order, the adapter layer restores search hit order; when the caller has specified order, preserve the ordering produced by ActiveRecord. The latter branch takes precedence because order expresses the caller's explicit business intent. The pagination offset only determines which slice of records to fetch and should not be treated as a sorting criterion; this change will not add any new sort parameters either.

This choice abandons the practice of treating the default relation order as an implicit contract for stable ordering. The hit order returned by the search service may change as the index contents change, but that is exactly the result already exposed to callers by searches with no sort specified. Conversely, if the adapter layer reorders records when no order is specified, callers cannot tell from the interface whether that order came from search or was supplied by the relation layer.

Regression tests should compare the records users ultimately receive, without tying themselves to internal helper methods. Test cases need to have a hit order that differs from the relation's default order: for calls without order, check that records remain in hit order; after adding an explicit order, check only that this order still takes effect. Existing paginated queries can cover both branches, but do not turn pagination behavior into a new ordering guarantee.

There are two rollback conditions: hit order is still being rearranged after the default-branch adjustment, or results with an explicit order are changed. If either occurs, remove the default-order handling and retain the original query path, pending further investigation of the mapping between the relation object and the search results. Start implementation verification at `elasticsearch-model/lib/elasticsearch/model/adapters/active_record.rb`; this round does not break down the specific changes within that file.

# Migration Notes for Empty Batches in Preprocessing

This page originally started from a call name, and only later did we realize that a call name and the actual migration boundary are not the same thing. `elasticsearch-model/lib/elasticsearch/model/adapters/active_record.rb` remains the most convenient local starting point, but the repository index labels it as an existing rb module for reading code and checking historical behavior. The old records located it through `orm`, `adapters`, `activerecord`, and `preprocess`, which does not mean they had already identified the full upstream and downstream.

An early working hypothesis is retained here: if there is no batch after preprocessing, execution may still go from `find_in_batches` into `block`, then continue sending downstream through `yield`. This claim was later narrowed. "Whether there is an empty batch", "whether the block executes", and "whether yield occurs" need to be treated as three separate observation points. Seeing only a method name cannot substitute for these three results; likewise, seeing a file path does not establish that the call relationships have been fully traced.

### Entry-Point Assessment in the Old Records

The initial reading order was fairly direct. First look for `find_in_batches`, assume it executes every time upon seeing `block`, then infer from `yield` that the caller has already received the data. This order is useful for quick navigation, but it hides the empty result after preprocessing in the middle. It remains here because it explains why this record once attributed the issue to the file entry point, not because that attribution has been proven correct.

At the time, "empty batch" in the issue description was also treated as a sufficiently well-defined object. It later became clear that at least three situations need to be distinguished: there is already no batch before preprocessing; preprocessing produces an empty value; a batch still exists after preprocessing, but no downstream result is observed. These three states may appear around the same set of call names, so the record cannot just say "empty batch". What this page can confirm is that these states need to be observed separately, and their order cannot be inferred from their names.

### Moving from the Old Investigation Method to Local Checks

The migration now is not about moving a confirmed implementation to another file, but about shifting the search boundary from the issue name and call name to the preprocessing result. First record the local declarations currently visible in `active_record.rb`, then record the batch state before and after preprocessing. Only after obtaining this local result should you check whether `block` is entered; if it is, then check whether `yield` occurs. This separates "no batch" from "nothing sent downstream".

Record the observations in the following order:

1. Preserve the state of the input batch without first classifying it as non-empty or empty.
2. Record the result after `preprocess` separately; if the result is empty, do not substitute a non-empty sample.
3. For an empty result, continue by checking whether `block` executes. If it is not entered, do not immediately record this as having been blocked.
4. If a block is observed, then confirm whether `yield` occurs, and record these two observations separately.
5. Check non-empty batches separately to establish the behavior of the normal path; they cannot be used as proof of the empty path.
6. If the current revision still does not clarify the reference relationships, return to `v_prev` and restore only that file's local declarations and adjacent locations.

This sequence adds one stopping point compared with the first draft: the value after preprocessing. It is not an additional processing stage, but a way to prevent empty results, block, and yield from being strung together into a single unobserved path. If only method names in the file are available, stop the record at those method names; if only local code is available and there are no caller results, do not fill in runtime results either.

```text
Old investigation method
Issue name / call name
       |
       v
active_record.rb
       |
Assume find_in_batches -> block -> yield

Current investigation method
Local declarations of active_record.rb
       |
       v
Batch state after preprocess
       +-- Non-empty -> actual block / yield results
       +-- Empty -> actual result of whether sending downstream continues
```

The two branches in the diagram represent the observation order, not confirmation of the implementation flow. The old investigation method retains the word "Assume"; the current method places the results that need to be obtained at the ends of the branches. There is no separate, frozen target file to list here, so "post-migration target location" can only mean this local inspection boundary, and must not be fabricated as a new module path.

The historical actions for ERX-214 provide the only explicit environment-related fork in this record. This also corrects an implicit skipped step in the first draft: no output does not mean the code did not execute; a permission failure also does not mean preprocessing returned an empty result. # ActiveRecord Ordering Decision Record

The original record addressed only a narrow issue: after search hits enter an ActiveRecord relation, the compatibility layer must not silently undo the ordering the caller has already specified. During the later review, the dispute was not about whether search results have an order, but about who expresses the final intent when two orders coexist.

Code review still starts at `elasticsearch-model/lib/elasticsearch/model/adapters/active_record.rb`. This location makes the ActiveRecord adapter the starting point for tracing ordering issues, but does not attribute all result assembly to a single file. The relation scope, search hit order, pagination offset, and the way records are retrieved converge along the same path; this record establishes only which choice to make when they conflict.

The initial draft's conclusion is retained as the policy for the 2026.7 compatibility release: when the relation has an explicit order, that order takes precedence; when it has no explicit order, restore the search hit order. The incidental order in which results happen to be retrieved is no longer treated as the default rule here.

## Paths Compared at the Time

The hit order of search results is not a meaningless intermediate state. It represents the ordering of results from a search that has already been executed; when the relation specifies no other order, returning records in that order keeps the record order seen by the caller aligned with the hit list just received. This branch does not require adding an extra ActiveRecord order.

On the other hand, explicit ordering on a relation is not decoration that can be ignored. By specifying an order in the relation, the caller has already chosen how records should be arranged. If the compatibility layer forcibly retrieves or reassembles records according to hit order in a later step, the caller will receive the correct set of records but will be unable to infer the final order from how the relation is written. The issue is not that the search order is invalid, but that the compatibility layer should not cancel a choice the caller has already expressed.

For that reason, "hit order always takes precedence" was not adopted. This approach is easy to explain, but it would turn explicit relation order into disposable information. Once existing ActiveRecord queries are connected to search results, the compatibility layer would change the result order, and the caller would have no way to prevent that change.

Nor was "raise an error whenever both orders exist" adopted. The coexistence of two orders is not itself an error: the relation has already established precedence. Turning it into a failure would create a restriction that exists only in the compatibility layer, without helping the caller retrieve records that could otherwise be returned.

A looser approach also came up during review: retain both orders and let different call sites decide which one to use. It was not adopted. This would give the same relation different defaults under different integration approaches, turning a choice that should be explicit in the relation into a hidden difference between calls. 2026.7 does not add this kind of dispatch.

## Established Boundaries

Here, "explicit ordering" means that the relation already carries ordering intent supplied by the caller; the hit order naturally produced by the search side does not count as ordering on the relation. Here, "restoring hit order" describes only the choice of how records are arranged when they enter the returned result; it does not extend to the search request's ordering strategy or change the index-side default behavior.

This distinction puts the two kinds of information back in their respective places: relation order is the caller's requirement for records, while hit order is the search result ordering that can be retained when there is no contrary requirement. Both can exist, but they cannot both serve as the final ordering basis for the same set of records.

Pagination offset is a related condition that requires separate review. It may cause an ordering issue to appear as missing records, duplicate records, or an apparent change in ordering between pages. This condition does not change precedence itself; the review should focus on confirming that the ordering choice occurs at the correct stage, rather than attempting to fix it after records have already been fixed in place according to another basis.

The approach of "sorting again" at the end of the returned object is not adopted. The final records are where the symptoms are easiest to see, but that does not mean the ordering conflict should be handled at the end. If an earlier part of the relation path has already selected hit order or relation order, reordering at the end would overlap with pagination, scope conditions, and reuse of the response from an already executed search. The problem would shift from an order mismatch to a situation where both the record set and page boundaries are difficult to explain.

Response-object branches should not become places to patch ordering either. The ordering decision concerns the arrangement of records, not replacing the source of search results. When existing callers depend on `raw_response`, the ordering branch must not wrap it in another response object and then lead callers to mistake an object change for an ordering change.

Dynamic Response Field Method Lookup is a related topic and remains in the materials for DOC-26. This decision adds no rules for method dispatch; it only requires that the ordering implementation not use response-object branches to bypass the ordering already expressed by the relation.

## Execution Gaps Left by the Review

ERX-216 was originally intended to add a record that directly triggers this scenario: use the existing entry point to save the input and the tool's actual output. It was blocked in the target environment, with the recorded reason being that the account supplied by the caller lacked permissions. The item later returned to the backlog because the owner was out this week, so it would no longer occupy an in-progress slot.

This experience did not overturn the ordering decision, nor can it serve as proof that the ordering path has run successfully. It explains why the current record still focuses on the decision and code entry points rather than including a complete execution result. When this work resumes, the record needs to include whether the relation has explicit ordering, the ordering of the search results, and the order of the records actually returned; recording only pass or fail will not reveal which side the conflict occurred on.

The card's history can be summarized by the following state changes. They record an interruption in adding execution evidence, not a change to the ordering rules.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> To_Do
    To_Do --> Blocked: Caller account lacks permissions
    Blocked --> To_Do: Owner is out this week
```

When execution evidence is missing, we should not revert to the old assumption that "hit order always takes precedence." Ordering precedence comes from the trade-off made at the compatibility boundary; execution records confirm whether the actual path honors that trade-off. The two pieces need to be completed separately.

## Compatibility Items Not Included in the Ordering Branch

The removed persistence entry point and ActiveRecord ordering are separate issues. Loading the `Elasticsearch::Persistence::Model` persistence mode should raise `LoadError`, and the constant should not be defined. This behavior is not determined by the ordering branch, and old constants or entry points should not be retained in the adapter merely to avoid a load failure.

Document types, typeless request, partial updates, import batches, and the index lifecycle do not automatically acquire new ordering rules as a result of this decision either. They may belong to the same compatibility release, but they should not be included in the conflict path between relation and hit order. Otherwise, later investigations could misidentify unrelated changes as ordering regressions.

The current choice has a straightforward meaning: search results without explicit relation ordering continue to arrange records by hit order; when callers need a different order, they should express it explicitly on the relation. The compatibility layer neither guesses unstated preferences nor overrides stated ones.

## Points to Watch During Implementation Review

- In the actual records assembly path, confirm that whether the relation already has an order is identified before hit order is selected, rather than checked after records have already been fixed in hit order.
- When pagination offset is involved in the relation, neither branch may use the other branch's ordering basis.
- After ERX-216 resumes, retain at least the actual records order for the same search result under both a relation with no ordering and a relation with explicit ordering.
- If the review finds that the current call does not pass through the ActiveRecord adapter, add the new call location and correct the description of the entry point here.

The decision has established precedence; what remains is to align it with the actual execution path and the missing execution evidence.

# Dynamic Field Lookup Proposal

The first version began with a string of terms left over from the interface review. `response::result`, `result`, `respond_to`, and `method` appeared together in an earlier investigation, so `elasticsearch-model/lib/elasticsearch/model/response/pagination.rb` was treated as a priority place to look. The assumption at the time was that paginated responses probably retrieved dynamic fields through the same method lookup mechanism.

The available examples have not fully confirmed that assumption. It remains here because future reviews of the old discussions will still turn up the same path, but it is no longer enough to establish where field access occurs. The file is currently useful only as a starting point for reading the existing Ruby module and a reference for historical checks. Similarities among the filename, issue title, and call name do not mean that the file is responsible for implementing all response fields.

After review, the first step is to separate two questions: whether an object declares a given dynamic field, and which layer should interpret the value returned when the field is accessible. The former can be checked on the response object with a capability check; the latter cannot be determined from the field name alone. In particular, if the wrapper layer collapses a null value and a missing field into the same result, callers cannot recover the original distinction later.

**Candidate approach: check before reading**

Keep the core of the old proposal: first use `respond_to` to check whether the object can handle the target field, then access the field through `method`. This avoids having to enumerate the full field set in advance and suits cases where names vary by response. That is also where its drawback lies: there is no agreement yet on whether to return null, skip the field, or expose the failure to the caller when the check fails. Treating any one of these as the default would decide semantics for existing callers without evidence.

Checking and accessing are also distinct operations. If response wrapping or object replacement occurs in between, the earlier capability check does not automatically establish that the later access will still be valid. No failure output is available, and there is not enough material to specify an exception format. Tests should retain at least three distinct cases: the field exists and has a value, the field exists but its value is null, and the field does not exist. These are not there to pad coverage numbers, but to decide whether null can continue to mean "no field".

**Another, smaller-scope option**

If further review shows that `result` is a stable result-holding object, field lookup can be organized solely around its public access methods, without building another mapping layer in the pagination wrapper. This would be a smaller change and would keep access points close to the object; the trade-off is that if paginated responses and regular results use different wrappers, callers may still receive different feedback for missing fields.

A fixed field mapping remains a fallback. It suits cases where the actual entry point has narrowed down the field set, and regression cases would be more straightforward; however, every added field requires updates to both the mapping and the tests. The available material has not established that the set is closed, so a mapping should not be the default. Only consider it if dynamic lookup cannot be triggered reliably and callers need a short-term path, and make clear that it will be replaced later.

The disagreement in this review is not about Ruby syntax, but about responsibility boundaries. Putting the check in the response wrapper layer would centralize handling of null values and missing fields; the risk is changing the behavior of existing response objects. Letting callers make their own checks would reduce the migration scope, but could leave fields with the same name subject to two sets of rules on paginated and non-paginated paths. The recommendation remains to confirm the actual access point first, rather than push cross-module changes based directly on the path's location.

An adjacent compatibility check also became mixed into the discussion: loading the removed `Elasticsearch::Persistence::Model` persistence mode should yield `LoadError` and should not define that constant. This shows that "missing method" and "old entry point cannot be loaded" are not the same problem; the fallback for the former must not mask the latter. The `raw_response` in the response material should also retain its original object identity; the dynamic field proposal should not replace the original response with a different container just to make access easier.

The criteria for backing out remain specific. If examples show that field access happens in another layer, withdraw the implementation assumption about `pagination.rb`; if a field that exists but has a null value cannot be reliably distinguished from a missing field, withdraw the idea of silently returning null; if regression behavior differs between the paginated path and regular results, retain the old call pattern and do not make unified wrapping a release prerequisite.

What is still missing is existing tests or examples that exercise the actual entry point, and a record explaining which user paths are not covered. Until that material is available, this proposal is limited to comparing candidates and identifying places to revisit; the old assumption that "the pagination file is the entry point" should not be treated as the current conclusion.

This checklist has continued to be used under the old assumption that "the window can be closed out independently": once the last result for client and example has been organized and the exit action is no longer linked to a new sample, the window can be closed. It was not used to decide whether to release; the corresponding owner's sign-off was still handled separately. This premise was not rewritten along with the additions later made to the page, so it is easy to mistake it for a complete condition during handoff.

The entry is still written as: `docs/adj-elasticsearch-model/release/elasticsearch-model-client-integration-exit-window-checklist.md`. The page contains both old ordering records and gaps, revision, and routing issues later added to cards; do not retroactively fill in a status from a card as a result that had already been recorded on the page at the time.

## Start an exit record first

- [ ] Find the last example for this client in this run and put the input and the result displayed on the page at the time into the same record.
- [ ] If the sample contains `raw_response`, preserve this field and its corresponding content exactly as-is. A summary may be written separately, but do not leave only the summary.
- [ ] When loading the removed `Elasticsearch::Persistence::Model` persistence mode produces `LoadError`, first leave the failure output beside the sample. The old checklist temporarily treats this kind of loading failure as a blocker within the window; it does not decide here whether the release fails.
- [ ] If no compatibility boundary is visible beside the sample, write "No boundary seen", then stop; do not infer a boundary from the client name.

Here, "last time" refers only to the last result visible in this integration session, and does not mean that the project will no longer make any calls after that. An older version once used consecutive explicit order on the page as the basis for this judgment: if the order was consecutive, the window was considered to have no omissions. This judgment remains in the checklist, but it cannot explain windows in between where no record was left.

## Window-closing actions

1. Review the last example. If there is no new result after it, first record "No new sample observed"; do not phrase this as saying that the client has stopped being used.
2. Check the exit action. If the action still points to the old exit, do not delete it just because the example is normal; first retain the pre-change routing record.
3. If custom serialization appears after the last result, leave the state as-is. The old practice was to treat it as a sign that wrap-up was not yet complete, and to perform no cleanup even if there was no new error.
4. Place the raw result and the manually compiled conclusion side by side. If they differ, preserve the difference; do not choose one and rewrite it as the other.
5. Only ask the corresponding owner to sign after the window record is complete. If the sign-off is missing, stop at "Exit record complete"; do not mark it as "Release complete".

These steps are the operational sequence left at the time, not a general rule for every client. In particular, step 3: it treated custom serialization as a blocking signal without stating whether it was caused by the sample format, integration adaptation, or exit action. The checklist later did not add a way to distinguish them, and it is still written here as before.

## Old Note Beside the Card

The description for ERXA-003 was to leave unrecorded windows blank. At one point, the old checklist interpreted a blank as "there was no action in that segment," so when closing a window it checked only whether the two adjacent examples were consecutive; this can make missing records look like normal gaps. The current page has not filled in the intermediate result in its place, and the old interpretation has not been removed.

ERXA-005 recorded that the current revision was inconsistent with the page's timing. The checklist still handles this by first proceeding in the order of the windows on the page, then treating revision as corroborating evidence. It does not specify which side to choose when they disagree; it only requires that the newer page value not be written back into the old window.

ERXA-007 once recorded a case that stopped upon reaching the exit entry. This made "being able to enter the exit" and "completing the exit action" two separate things: the former can only remain in the sample field, while the latter still requires an action record. The checklist did not add a method for collecting the second type of failed sample.

ERXA-009 included a counterexample for the old exit action. The fallback procedure used here remains very conservative: retain the old route before deletion; after deletion, if the last example can no longer be reproduced, restore the old route and reopen the window. This wording does not specify which client record to resume from after restoration, nor does it count successful restoration as release sign-off.

## Stop Point

Stop at the window if any of the following occurs:

- The last example has no original result;
- `raw_response` has only cleaned-up text remaining;
- `LoadError` has been recorded as an ordinary successful result;
- The exit action still points to the old route;
- The page order and current revision do not match, and no one can explain which timing should be used.

# Alternative Route Proposal for Callers

The comparison at the time was between two integration routes: continuing to use `pagination offset`, or splitting out `index lifecycle` on its own. Both could retain an entry point for caller integration testing, but what needed to be investigated when something went wrong differed. The former kept pagination position and call results on the same path, required little change, and made it easier for existing callers to keep running; the trade-off was that a pagination issue could also draw in lifecycle assessment. The latter kept the lifecycle separate, with clearer boundaries, but required rechecking the state callers received; the split itself could not be taken to mean compatibility was complete.

## Preference at the Time

The preference was to first try splitting out `index lifecycle`. This was not because it had already been shown to be more stable, but because the material described different failure exit paths for the two parts: when using the old pagination entry point, failures looked like position or result issues; after the split, failures had to be investigated through the lifecycle object and caller feedback. If both kinds of failure were still combined under a single entry point, it would be hard during integration testing to tell whether the parameters had failed to arrive or the caller had not accepted the object's state.

This preference did not become an active rule. There was no start date or confirmed owner; "trial" could only mean the window in the proposal, not that a switch had already happened. The review also required an input for the opposite case, to verify whether the old path should be retained if a caller explicitly rejected the split. That validation window was still open at the time.

## Rollback Points

If, during the trial, existing callers cannot be kept running, the failure exit paths still cannot be distinguished, or `regression matrix` cannot find a caller in active use, first stop adding integrations and do not expand the split further. Whether to restore only the old entry point remained undecided: restoring just the entry point could leave already-written branches in place, while rolling everything back would lose the call results obtained during the split. The rollback action needs to be decided after the opposite-case input has finished running; it cannot be written up in advance as a definite command.

## Open Questions on Record

- Who will provide a caller in active use as the starting point for `regression matrix`?
- Is "restoring only the old entry point" enough to clean up the state left after the split?
- If the opposite-case input fails, which portion of the caller results should be retained?

The file `docs/adj-elasticsearch-model/proposals/rejected-elasticsearch-model-client-integration-approach.md` remains the entry point for reviewing this old route. It records the proposal that was not adopted and the objections raised at the time; it does not indicate that the preference here was later adopted. If new caller options come up later, keep them in a separate version; do not overwrite this old record.

# Client Legacy Entry Point Migration Guide

This index initially recorded only two ways to make the change, and it was only after the integration side added several real samples that we discovered that "the entry point has been replaced" and "the caller has migrated away" are not the same thing. The former can be seen in the directory, while the latter requires going back to the actual usage sites in client and example. Maintenance still follows this distinction: the directory provides locations, while the migration records preserve each consumer's state across the legacy entry point, candidate entry points, and restoration points.

This does not fold in every similarly named side path. The index covers only elasticsearch-model-client-integration: legacy entry points, replacement locations, callers still using them, and the first current revision retained during restoration. Notes that cannot be verified from the materials remain in their original locations and are marked as old records; do not assume migration is complete just to make things look tidy.

```text
Legacy entry point
  │
  ├── Retain original call sample ──> Record results from the legacy entry point
  │
  └── Change only the entry point selection ──> Candidate location
                              ├── repository mixin
                              └── document type
                                      │
                         Mismatch ─────┘
                                      │
                                  Restore legacy entry point
```

## How records are kept in the index

Each row represents an actual consumer, not a directory name. First specify which legacy entry point it uses, then place a sample from client or example that can reproduce use of that entry point alongside it. List only `repository mixin` or `document type` that are already being compared as replacement locations; do not prematurely mark callers that have not yet reached either location as undergoing migration.

Samples must retain the original input. The integration side once reformatted results to make them easier to read and then compared them with the replacement entry point; this made it impossible to tell whether a difference came from the entry point change or from the reformatting. The index now retains the original input, the first result from the legacy entry point, and the first result from the replacement entry point. If the state of the second call also needs to be compared, note it separately in the comments on the same row, rather than replacing two observations with a single summary.

Do not use caller names and entry point names interchangeably either. A caller Fang Ke may still be using the legacy entry point while the directory already lists a replacement location; a replacement location may also exist without having received any usable samples yet. The former has not migrated away, while the latter is merely an optional path. Neither is a reason to retire the legacy entry point.

`DOC-27` contains local code-reading notes from around the entry point; this page uses it only to cross-check the objects around the current entry point, and does not treat those unfinished notes as a list of callers. What actually needs to be added to the migration index are samples from usage sites, post-restoration results, and the reasons callers have not yet migrated away.

## Retain the legacy entry point first

Before migration, first confirm that the legacy entry point can still be called unchanged. "Retain" here does not mean all new code must keep choosing it, but that restoration must have a path that has not been rewritten by the replacement approach. Legacy samples should be saved alongside replacement attempts, and in particular, do not overwrite the input used at the time with an example corrected later.

An early draft treated `instance proxy` as something that could be replaced as a whole. After review, this claim needs to be narrowed: it was only one path being compared at the time. If a caller depends on the selection mechanism bundled into the entry point, switching directly to `caller options` may change where execution stops on failure; if the caller only needs the objects provided by the replacement location, then `repository mixin` or `document type` is worth including in the same batch of comparisons. The index does not make this judgment on the caller's behalf, but only records the entry points it actually used.

For each attempt involving the legacy entry point, retain at least three things: the original call sample, the replacement location selected at the time, and the first visible result. If the original sample is missing, the record can be marked "pending replay", but the input must not be inferred from the directory name. If there is no replacement location, it can still be registered as a consumer of the legacy entry point; such records are more useful for planning migration batches than a list containing only new names.

Keeping the legacy entry point readable does not mean expanding its use. If a new integration has not explicitly chosen the legacy entry point, do not add it back into a new example just for restoration needs. The restoration channel and the default integration are two different things: the former is kept for returning to the original context when results are inconsistent, while the latter is determined only after each caller completes its comparison.

## Comparing the two candidate locations

`repository mixin` and `document type` are both candidate replacement locations, but they must not be put in the same cell and labeled "replaced". Change only one condition when recording a comparison: keep the same call sample, state clearly which location the entry point selection is being changed to this time, then examine the result and the failure location. If the call arguments, example, and entry point are changed at the same time, the index cannot tell which change caused the difference.

`caller options` is a part that needs to be considered separately in this round of comparisons. At the draft stage, splitting it out was thought to be enough to avoid the differences associated with `instance proxy`; the samples retained later showed that, even after splitting it out, it is still necessary to confirm whether the caller carried the original selection over to the new location. The index therefore added a note on "how the caller supplies the selection" instead of marking all callers as having been adapted across the board.

`repository mixin` is suitable for trial use when the consumer has already been located. Start with a real call sample and leave the legacy entry point unchanged; if the result from the replacement entry point is inconsistent with the legacy path, stop expanding this batch, and do not hide that inconsistency behind another caller's success. Stopping here means stopping at that consumer's migration step, not deleting the attempts already recorded.

Compare `document type` the same way, but do not assume it is interchangeable with `repository mixin`. These are simply the replacement locations listed in the current index. A sample working through one does not imply the other can handle it too; likewise, a failure at one location does not automatically mean the legacy entry point is no longer valid. Keeping these two candidates is intended to show, on later review, what was compared at the time, not to declare a universal replacement rule.

Early records treated differences in failure exit points as a reason to favor splitting `caller options`, and that judgment is still retained in the draft. The current use is more specific: different failure exit points only mean that this sample needs a separate comparison; whether to migrate still depends on the caller's first result from the replacement location and its restoration result.

## Do not advance batches by directory

A migration batch starts with a sample that points to an actual usage site. First find the legacy entry point row in the index, copy the original input, choose a candidate location, and then append the two results from the new and legacy entry points side by side. Move on to the next consumer only after completing this row. The reason for this is not to insist on row-by-row operations, but to avoid carrying one caller's adaptation boundaries over to another caller.

Rows with insufficient samples stay in the legacy entry point group. Do not borrow an input from a similarly named client or example just to form a complete batch. Migration records deal with actual call samples, not name matching. If all that can be confirmed is that the legacy entry point is still being used, the index should stop there; the maintainer may use this to schedule a replay, but cannot use it to declare the replacement location valid.

Post-restoration records have one additional constraint: starting from the restoration point, take only the first current revision. Do not add later summaries to this row for now. This restriction keeps the restoration result alongside the original context, rather than letting it be diluted by a subsequent series of normal or abnormal results. Do not overwrite the pre-restoration failure window or object either; leave them under the same caller entry for reference in the next comparison.

ERXA-008 remind us to replay using the original elasticsearch-model-client-integration input, not to reconstruct a sample that merely looks similar. ERXA-010 require the restoration result to be appended to the index, with the original failure window and object retained. ERXA-012 limit post-restoration capture to the first current revision; ERXA-014 keep this migration trail in this index, with only a link in the daily report. These four cards provide navigation for the migration records, not a replacement for the samples and results in each row.

## Restoration when results are inconsistent

If the result under `document type` is inconsistent with the legacy entry point, first stop further attempts for that caller at the candidate location, restore the legacy entry point, then check once more with the same original input. Append the first current revision after restoration alongside the original result. There is no requirement here to immediately explain where the difference came from; restore the legacy path first to avoid continuing to expand the migration scope in an already inconsistent state.

Restoration records cannot just say "restored". At a minimum, they must show which caller was restored, which legacy entry point it returned to, whether the original input was reused, and where the first current revision was retained. If the original input can no longer be found, preserve that gap rather than replacing it with a new example. A new example may become a candidate sample later, but it cannot rewrite the original failure window.

For a time, the practice was: as long as the replacement location was accessible, mark the legacy entry point as removable. That practice no longer applies. Accessibility only means the candidate location can be entered, not that callers still using the legacy entry point have obtained the same results, nor that the restoration path has been verified. The old passage is kept here to explain why the index now records "the replacement location exists", "the caller has completed a comparison", and "restoration has been recorded" separately.

Rolling back does not mean deleting the replacement attempts either. Failed attempts, restoration actions, and the original object should all remain in the same migration record. Otherwise, the next time the legacy entry point is seen still in use, it is easy to misinterpret this as a migration that never started, rather than one that was rolled back because of inconsistent results.

## Closing a legacy entry point record

Move a caller from the legacy entry point group to the migrated group only when all three conditions hold: the replacement location has been specified; the caller's sample has been compared; and any records left when restoration was needed can also be reviewed. A new entry point appearing in the directory, an unrelated sample passing, or a migration link appearing in the daily report is not sufficient on its own to close the record.

Do not force closure on old notes that cannot be verified. Keep them in the index, separate from rows that already have samples. This lets readers see which content comes from actual replays and which is merely a historical pointer to an entry point. The independent schedule, maintainer, and exit criteria remain attached to this project and are not replaced by the main project's summary.

The current maintenance entry point is `docs/adj-elasticsearch-model/migration/current-entry-legacy-entry-migration-index.md`. When adding records later, prioritize callers still using the legacy entry point and the first current revision after restoration; do not overwrite this migration trail accumulated sample by sample with a new directory.

# Quality Signal Handoff Troubleshooting Tree

When a quality signal stalls at an entry point, don't rerun right away. First return the failing sample from that test or spec run to its original location, then decide whether to stay in elasticsearch-persistence-quality-signal or exit.

```text
Any failing samples at this entry point?
├─ No: stop. Collect the missing original input, current revision, and first result.
└─ Yes: check whether you can find a normal sample from the same run.
   ├─ Can't find one: stay at the quality signal desk for now; don't guess about index lifecycle.
   └─ Found one: look only at the first difference.
      ├─ The difference is within the project: keep investigating
      └─ The difference crosses an interface: hand it off
```

The old habit was to clean up and rerun whenever a regression matrix appeared; that mixes the first failure with a later green result. Preserve the original record first. Even when `typeless request` hasn't appeared, don't infer from the directory name that the request is already correct.

If the signal itself has no raw record, don't exit yet. If only aggregate numbers remain, collect the missing data and stop; don't use averages to decide who takes over.

When you can find a normal sample, compare only the first difference at the same entry point. Don't change the import batch and adjust custom serialization at the same time, then write up the final result as a single cause. document type is only a possible location in the record, not grounds for handing off the sample immediately.

The earliest note treated `index lifecycle` as the first branch. That was just a convenient search term at the time. If the original input, current revision, or first result is missing, stop at data collection; leave the index, request, and serialization for inspection once you have a comparison sample.

When exiting this investigation, also record the point you reached. An exit entry point that hasn't been run does not count as complete, and you must not delete the failing sample just to free up the entry point. When a rerun goes green, append that result to the old record rather than replacing it.

# Quality Signal Handoff Troubleshooting Tree

When the quality signal console gets stuck, the most common wrong move is not making the wrong judgment, but replacing the original failure state: rerunning it, overwriting the old input with new artifacts, or attributing the failure to the index first. This tree preserves the paths through the on-call entry points used at the time. Several sections no longer apply to today's entry points, but old links still lead people here, so they have not been deleted.

Start with what is visible from the current entry point. Here, the "current entry point" is the one where a test or spec failure is triggered, a trend breaks, normal access is denied, or the on-call responder cannot continue an exit action; it is not one particular fixed page. Once the entry point changes, the old statistics can still be kept as clues, but they cannot automatically be carried over to the new entry point.

```text
Quality signal stalled
│
├─ Is there an original failing sample?
│  ├─ No
│  │  ├─ Can the original input, current revision, and first result be restored?
│  │  │  ├─ Yes: Restore them, then restart from the top of the tree
│  │  │  └─ No: Stay at the quality signal console and stop root-cause assessment
│  │  └─ Do not replace the original failure state with a new green sample
│  │
│  └─ Yes
│     ├─ Is the sample from the current worker?
│     │  ├─ Uncertain: Verify first, do not hand off
│     │  └─ Yes: Find a normal sample from the same round and the same entry point
│     │
│     ├─ Is the first divergence still within the test/spec project?
│     │  ├─ Yes: Stay at elasticsearch-persistence-quality-signal
│     │  └─ No: Check whether the divergence concerns an exit action or a permission denial
│     │
│     ├─ Did the exit action fail to complete?
│     │  └─ Yes: Preserve the node already reached, and investigate the exit entry point separately
│     │
│     └─ Was non-admin access denied?
│        ├─ Yes: Record the denial location and the request/run id, and hand off to the permissions owner
│        └─ No: Only hand off to the shared entry point once outside a clearly defined interface
```

This tree does not require naming the failure first. First establish that the records in hand really belong to this particular stall, then discuss whether it resembles index, request, or serialization issues seen before. Without the original failure state, what you can do is restore the records, not fill in an explanation for that state.

## The First Sign Is a Break in the Trend

You cannot directly subtract the before-and-after values in a trend chart, especially when the current entry point has just changed. The reminder from ERXB-002 is to first mark where the entry point changed; old statistics can be kept as clues, but they cannot be joined with the post-change statistics into one continuous trend.

In this situation, do two things first: find the last failing or normal sample before the entry point changed; then find the first result after the change, and save the original inputs from the two sides separately. The two sets of records do not have to match. They are used only to determine whether the signal started losing comparability at the entry point change.

If the samples before and after the change point are not even the same kind of input, stop the tree here. Do not work backward from directory names, the final display, or later aggregate counts to intermediate requests just to explain the trend. A trend can suggest that "re-stratification is needed"; it cannot prove that a particular test, spec, or index is already wrong.

At one point, the on-call guidance directly labeled this situation as a `index lifecycle` issue. That was an old marker left to narrow the scope, not a conclusion. When the entry point itself changes, first check the samples' sources and where they fall in time; continue investigating in that direction only if the first difference is already near the index.

A normal sample from before the entry point changed is not a universal control either. It only shows that, before the change, one record was able to reach a certain point. If that sample has no original input, no corresponding current revision, or only aggregate numbers left, do not put it in the same comparison group as the new failure. Stay on the trend branch and complete the records before deciding whether there is a regression.

## First preserve the original state

The original state must at least let the person taking over identify three things: the original input received at the time, the current revision used at the time, and the first visible result. Keep subsequent cleanup, reruns, rollbacks, and new artifacts separate, and do not let them overwrite these three items.

The records for ERXB-006 led to this rule being added because the original state was no longer available. If all that remains is a cleaned-up successful sample, do not treat it as evidence of recovery from the failure. At most, it shows that some later run no longer displayed the same symptom, but it cannot show which branch it originally got stuck on.

When something is missing, proceed as follows:

```text
Original state missing
├─ Part of the failure output is still available
│  ├─ Can confirm it corresponds to the current worker: mark it as an incomplete sample and continue comparing to find the first difference
│  └─ Cannot confirm: record only that the source is unknown; do not use it to attribute the cause
├─ Only a cleaned-up green result remains
│  └─ Do not use as evidence of recovery; return to the collection entry point
└─ Original input has been rolled back
   ├─ Due action still points to the new artifact: record the two things separately
   └─ Cannot find the pre-rollback content: stop at "original state unavailable"
```

"The original input has been rolled back, but the due action still points to the new artifact" was once handled as a single release issue, but it was later found that this conflated two lines of investigation: one was whether the original input could still reproduce the failure, and the other was what the pending action actually pointed to. Keep both lines of investigation, but do not use one to make judgments about the other.

After the original input is rolled back, the new artifact may still continue to be referenced by some due action. This does not mean the old failure has moved elsewhere, nor does it mean the new artifact caused the old failure. In the record, simply put "whether the pre-rollback content can be found" and "where subsequent actions point" next to each other, and do not combine them into a single status.

If `raw_response` appears in the record, keep it together with the first failure result, and do not extract only the few lines that look like the cause of the error. Someone on call once copied the easily readable part of a response into the summary, and the original fragment disappeared during cleanup; afterward, it was impossible to determine whether the difference was caused by the response content, the input conditions, or the collection point.

Keeping the original fragment does not require understanding it immediately. The purpose here is only to ensure that the next comparison still has the same starting point. If the response fragment and the failure output come from different workers, both can be saved, but their sources must be labeled separately; do not splice them into what looks like a complete record.

## When a sample is mislabeled, do not keep branching

ERXB-013 had one clear mislabeling: the seemingly complete original input came from another worker. This is more dangerous than "no sample" because it can easily lead someone to continue onward.

When the sample's worker source is unclear, stop at source verification. Do not compare document type, do not inspect custom serialization, and do not use this to claim that the regression has been isolated to a particular spec. Once the source is confirmed, the comparison should still do only one thing: find a normal sample from the same run and entry point, and inspect the first place where they differ.

"First difference" means the first position in the record sequence that cannot be aligned; it is not the name of the failure that appears last. It may be the original input, runtime environment, request, failure output, or the state before the exit action. Do not explain later differences yet, to avoid letting one error make the entire log appear to have the same cause.

"Same run" is meant to prevent an old green result from being treated as evidence from the current incident; it does not require collecting a complete set of historical samples every time. If no normal sample can be found for the current run, retain only the failed sample and the gap. Do not substitute an old fragment of unclear origin just to create a comparison.

Below is a common wrong path from old on-call records:

```text
Failure output exists
└─ See document type
   └─ Hand directly to the storage side
```

This path is now retained only as a counterexample. document type is one possible lead, not a basis for handoff. When the sample comes from the wrong worker, even the "first difference" has not yet been established; handing it to the storage side first only means the other party receives a fragment with nothing to compare it against.

Another mistake is to see `repository mixin` and treat it as a normal sample. This label can help find a comparison object, but it cannot guarantee that the object and the failed sample are from the same entry point or the same run. The same label with different sources still cannot be compared. It is not a substitute for sample identity.

## Project-internal signals: do not broaden the scope yet

Only when the original input, current revision, first result, and sample source all line up should you check whether the failure still falls within the scope of elasticsearch-persistence-quality-signal. Failure samples produced by test or spec, regression stratification, and flaky-signal attribution should all be organized here first; do not route the issue to another project prematurely just because the final output contains an Elasticsearch-related term.

For an in-project investigation, the smallest comparison unit is one failure and one recent normal sample. Change only one condition at a time. If narrowing the scope requires changing the entry point, sample, and runtime environment at the same time, do not write up the result as a single cause.

Here, "one condition" does not mean that each run can produce only one record. It means that during comparison, only one factor may be designated as different. For example, if you already know the entry point changed, you cannot also change the worker and then claim that the difference comes from the entry point; if you need to verify the worker, do not simultaneously replace the old original input with a new artifact. If this cannot be done, leave the changes listed in parallel; do not force an order.

An old page once advised: "After seeing the regression matrix, do not clean up the scene." This is still useful, but it originally did not make clear why. The matrix merely lays samples out by regression tier; it cannot replace the first failed input, nor can it verify whether a sample came from the current worker. After seeing the matrix, first recheck the original scene, then decide whether to use it for stratification.

If the matrix contains only final red/green results, with no failure snippets, original input, or source, then it is suitable only for marking "this is worth capturing again." Do not infer directly from a red row that a particular request is incompatible, nor check it off with a later green row. The quality signal desk retains the relationship between tiers and samples, rather than simply storing the most recent status.

Sometimes the signal turns green after a rerun. This result can be appended to the original failure, but it must not be used to delete the failure. If the green result appeared after cleaning up the scene, switching the entry point, rolling back the input, or changing the worker, it describes a later run, not that the initial hang has been explained.

The old records also contain one premature retry. After the retry, only cleaned-up output remained, and the original failure location could no longer be matched. This lesson does not imply "never rerun": when the original scene has been preserved, the sample source has been confirmed, and the comparison node has also been documented, a later run can still be performed; it must simply remain afterward as a new record.

## Ordinary Access Denied

When access to adj-elasticsearch-persistence under a non-admin identity is denied, do not write it up as a quality signal failure yet. The local action for ERXB-013 requires leaving the denial location and request/run id on the original card; this lets the permission owner determine whether the denial occurred at the entry point, on the detail page, or before a subsequent action.

This branch is short:

```text
Ordinary entry-point access failed
├─ Denial location + request/run id present
│  └─ Hand off to the permission owner; the quality signal desk retains only the associated failed sample
└─ No
   └─ Fill in these two items first; do not assess the permission configuration
```

The denial location must be recorded at the step where the ordinary identity can no longer proceed, not merely as "access failed." If the denial occurs immediately upon entering the entry point, versus only after the detail page can be reached, those are different handoff materials; without a location, the permissions side also cannot tell where to take over.

Do not use successful administrator access to negate ordinary-access denial. They use different identities, and the administrator result only shows that an administrator can enter. Do not combine one denial with the failed sample of test/spec into a single root cause either, unless they show a clear first difference at the same entry point and in the same scene.

When ordinary access fails, the quality signal desk still retains the failed sample it already has. What the permissions side receives is the denial location and request/run id, not the entire sample being archived and moved away. If the ordinary entry point recovers but the original test still fails, return to the project-side branch; if all that is confirmed is that an administrator can enter, the branch remains at ordinary-access denied.

Later additions made this section clearer than the old draft, but it is still not a complete guide to permission operations. Instructions on how the permissions owner makes changes and verifies them after taking over remain in the permissions-side documentation; this page only hands off the rejection point and related records.

## Exit action stuck

"The person on duty only got halfway through, and the subsequent exit entry point was not run" is another type of stopping point. It does not mean that the original issue has already been handed over to someone else, nor does it mean that the preceding part has already recovered. Keep the completed nodes, and mark the exit entry point that has not been run separately.

```text
Need to exit the current troubleshooting process
├─ Exit entry point has finished running
│  └─ End this round's record based on the actual result
├─ Partway through
│  └─ Retain completed nodes; do not fill in the record as though the exit were complete
└─ Not yet started
   └─ Preserve the current state, and resume once the entry point becomes available
```

Here, "exit" means the action of leaving the current troubleshooting path, not deleting failed samples or automatically closing the issue. When the exit entry point has not been run, the person taking over needs to know what was done before and which layer it stopped at; therefore, recording only "incomplete" is not enough, and at a minimum, the completed nodes and the entry point that was not entered must be retained.

In the past, someone cleared the failed samples first when "partway through", on the grounds that the exit action would regenerate the data. This left those who came later seeing only a partial exit status, without being able to see why an exit was needed. That old reminder is still retained: preserve the original state before exiting; but it is no longer required to keep the current entry point occupied indefinitely just to retain samples. When the evidence is complete but the exit entry point has not been run, simply stop at the exit branch.

Even if a new green status appears after the exit action has started, the status still cannot automatically be rewritten as "exit successful". The green status may belong to a later run segment, while the exit entry point may still not have been reached. Record both side by side: where the state from the earlier segment was saved, and how far the exit action in the later segment actually progressed. Do not use green status in place of the action's status.

This is also why this page does not list "rerun" as a recovery step. Rerunning may be part of subsequent operations, but when the original state has not been saved, the exit is incomplete, or the sample source is unclear, it will only generate another record with a different context.

## Outdated index branch

The following passage comes from the earliest field notes and is retained for people arriving from old links. Its conclusions are too strong, so it can no longer be followed directly.

> When you see `index lifecycle`, check the index; if you see that `typeless request` is missing, stop; if document type appears, hand off to the corresponding owner.

At the time, this passage treated several terms that often appeared together as a troubleshooting sequence. Later records showed that entry point changes, samples from the wrong worker, and unfinished exit actions could all appear before these terms. The old branch can now only serve as a search lead: if the first difference has already been confirmed to be near the relevant request or index, then investigate it; otherwise, do not jump from a name to a conclusion about the cause.

The early notes also treated import batch as a natural boundary: as soon as the batch changed, start treating it as an index issue again. This approach is likewise no longer reliable. The batch can indicate which part of the import a record came from, but it cannot prove that the request, sample source, or failure point is the same. When the original input has not been preserved, do not reconstruct a comparison chain from the batch name.

custom serialization was also once listed at the end of the old tree. It is retained because older records lead here using this term, not because seeing it means you should leave the quality signal desk. First confirm whether it is the first point that cannot be aligned across samples from the same run; if it appears only in output that was organized later, return to the original evidence first.

The old branches are useful only as reminders to the person on call that these terms have appeared before. They cannot replace the current sequence: original evidence, sample source, same-run comparison, first difference, and only then the specific object. Putting old terms first often causes people to overlook records that have already been lost earlier in the process.

## Do not merge the loading path into the indexing branch

Sometimes the quality signal stalls during loading. If importing a removed persistence mode produces `LoadError`, treat that output as evidence from the loading path, do not add a constant definition based on it, and do not recast it as an indexing exception. This branch only indicates that loading did not complete; any later handoff concerning a possible compatibility interface must wait until the interface boundary is clear.

This constraint was added after the old manual grouped "loading failure" and "indexing failure" together. Both can cause the quality signal to stall, but the former stops first in the loading path, so do not continue down the indexing branch just because the names are similar.

When the loading path has failure output but no original input, the procedure remains unchanged: preserve the output first, then start again from the top of the tree if the original input can be recovered; if it cannot, record only that processing stopped during loading. Do not use a different record that loads successfully as proof that this particular failure has been resolved.

Likewise, an error in the loading path does not automatically mean that an ordinary access denial is related to it. Both types of symptoms may be displayed by the same entry point, but without samples from the same run and the first difference, they must remain in their respective branches. Merging them would send the permissions owner a loading fragment that does not belong to permission evaluation.

## When handling outside the interface is needed

Route the issue beyond this page only when the samples within the project have been aligned and the first difference clearly crosses the current interface boundary. When handing it off, attach the evidence already preserved, not a string of guesses:

- The original input and current revision;
- The first failure result, and the preserved `raw_response` (if any);
- A normal sample from the same run and the first point of difference;
- Whether there is an entry point change, a wrong worker, an ordinary access denial, or an exit action that has not finished.

These items are not intended to make the person taking over walk through the tree again. They show how far this page has been followed and which conditions have not yet been ruled out. If an item is missing, simply state that it is missing; do not fill in an answer from trend summaries, directory names, or administrator access results just to make the handoff look complete.

"Clearly crosses the current interface boundary" is not established merely by seeing an external object name. You first need aligned samples, and must confirm that the first difference is not in a test, spec, collection point, or exit node within the current project. Otherwise, the issue should remain in elasticsearch-persistence-quality-signal, even if the term ultimately displayed appears to belong to another side.

When handing off a permission denial, include the denial location and request/run id; when handing off a loading failure, include the output from the loading stage; when handing off a difference between aligned samples, include the first point of difference. Do not replace these three different types of evidence with a generic description.

## Handoff point

This page's original handoff entry point was `docs/adj-elasticsearch-persistence/runbooks/elasticsearch-persistence-quality-signal-blocked-escalation-contacts.md`. Older records still reference that path, but the page content and attachments are maintained by elasticsearch persistence · Quality Signal Board. If you find an explicit permission denial, hand it off to the permissions owner; if you find unstable test/spec samples within the project, keep it at the quality signal desk; only use the shared entry point if you find that the issue has already crossed the interface boundary and the incident context is complete.

DOC-35 records the temporary handoff boundaries and can be used to confirm the handoff target; it does not replace the assessment of the incident context here. ERXB-002, ERXB-006 and ERXB-013 retain navigation points for non-comparable trends, missing original incident context and standard entry-point denials respectively. Status changes on the cards should not overwrite the failure samples already saved on this page.

At the time of the last maintenance update, the old tree's "look at the call edge first" sequence was already no longer reliable. The current order is to first verify the original incident context, then verify the sample source, and only then compare the first point of difference. If new entry-point types appear later, create a separate branch; do not put them back into the index lifecycle section.

# Gemfile Entry-Point Tracing Workflow

This record retains the old term "current entry point." The original intent was only to get from the public entry point for Gemfile · Package Integration to the current revision corresponding to gemfile-package-integration. At the time, the entry point was treated as a single path. After the navigation changed, the old draft wasn't rewritten as new guidance; only a few notes were added in place.

> Old route: Open `docs/adj-gemfile/notes/from-current-entry-to-current-revision.md`, locate the item under "current entry point," and start by following the first direct caller; if the name matches, keep recording the trace through to the current revision. The old draft treated this sequence as a sufficient path for tracing back.

That assumption is no longer reliable. The requirement from ERXD-001 is to keep separate records for the two entry points with the same name, distinguished by source and adopter. The item that appears first in navigation isn't necessarily the one being sought; "first" in the old draft was just the browsing order at the time, not an object relationship.

When reviewing this record, still start from the path above. First confirm whether the item under that path refers to the current entry point or an old entry point that hasn't yet been removed. When entries have the same name, don't merge them by name: only move on to checking the adopter once the sources match; if the sources differ, keep them separate even if they ultimately point to similar version combinations. Only when both the source and adopter match should the entry be put in the same record as gemfile-package-integration.

The old draft also took too narrow a view. It interpreted "reaching the current revision" as finding a destination with the same name, without separately recording cross-package dependencies, version combinations, and consumer-side integration. This makes it easy to read this and assume that a single Gemfile name represents the whole combination; that old interpretation remains on the page and hasn't been rewritten as new entry-point guidance.

ERXD-004 require cleanup of the outdated current-entry-point navigation while keeping the original "from current entry point to current revision" record and its date available for reference. Don't delete this record when removing the navigation; it explains how the old navigation used names as paths. It still refers to "current entry point" in the singular and does not include the two entry points resulting from the split.

For this review, keep a record in three columns: source, call edge, and adopter. First record the source path exactly as it is, then follow the direct call relationships to the first consumer; if no call edge can be found, stop at the current node and don't jump just because a file has the same name. Finally, record the resolved revision and version combination separately, and leave unverified adopter information blank. This way, even if the old navigation is subsequently removed, the two entry points seen at the time can still be reconstructed from the date and source.
