# Gemfile Package Integration Status Review

This incident occurred in the cross-package dependencies built around Gemfile. During consumer integration, the same version combination showed different current revisions at two points in time. The old record and the recovery page each captured some of the results, but the differences between the two could not be tied to a single cause at the time.

## Timeline

- During the initial check of the version combination, the old record was still accessible through the entry point. In the first comparison, raw_response differed from the old record; the difference was not just in display order.
- Checking the current entry point again then returned a different current revision. This was tentatively attributed to a delayed entry point refresh, but no timestamp was retained that could confirm that assessment.
- After the integration side tried a partial update, reads recovered, so further retries were stopped. Recovery only showed that this path worked at the time; it did not explain why the two results differed.
- The old record mentioned a change in hit order. This persisted after recovery, and there was not enough evidence to determine whether it shared a cause with the revision difference.

## Impact

The affected consumers were those integrating with this Gemfile version combination: for the same object, the record, the entry point, and the recovery result could not be used directly in place of one another. Looking only at the last successful read during investigation would obscure the earlier differences; following only the old record would lead to a revision that had already changed. The original record is retained at `docs/adj-gemfile/incidents/Gemfile-package-integration-two-states-for-one-object.md` as a starting point for reviewing what was observed at the time.

## Recorded Assessment

The approach taken at the time was to retain the original record and the recovery page, and to stop treating the partial update as a root-cause fix. The old page's "delayed entry point refresh" was only a working assessment. No supporting evidence was obtained later, so it cannot serve as a reliable explanation for the version combination.

Missing timestamp: ____

Still unconfirmed: which stage supplied each of the two current revisions, and whether the hit order changed in the same update.

# Package Integration Exit Window Procedure

The previous version left only "don't clean up yet" and an untested recovery gap. Records added later show that the execution details visible within the window do not always let us reconstruct the sequence: in some places, only aggregate results remain, with no intermediate events retained; the hash at the exit entry point also differs from the execution record, and the original download entry point has been disabled. This version therefore breaks window closure into a series of checks where we can stop, rather than treating a single green record as a completed exit.

This page covers only the exit action for `gemfile-package-integration`, the last visible result, and the local records for adj-gemfile. It does not determine whether the release succeeded; the corresponding owner still needs to sign off. Anyone taking over temporarily is responsible only for the action at hand. If a long-term owner is still not registered, the window handoff cannot be recorded as long-term ownership.

## What to keep when opening the window

1. [ ] Open `docs/adj-gemfile/release/gemfile-package-integration-exit-window-checklist.md`, confirm you are using the current version of the checklist for this window, and save the entry point alongside the record for this window. This path is where to look when taking over, not a common entry point for all package integrations.
2. [ ] State that this window checks only the exit action, the last visible result, and the exit record for adj-gemfile. If someone also asks for confirmation of consumer integration or cross-package version combinations, leave that part at its original workflow entry point; do not assess it in passing in this window.
3. [ ] Save the original input and the first result you see. If the execution record provides only aggregate results, explicitly mark it "event sequence not retained"; do not use an aggregated success indicator to fill in a sequence that does not exist.
4. [ ] Leave missing intermediate records blank. A blank is not a completion state that can be inferred from adjacent windows, and should not be tidied up into "no issues" before closing the window.

Here, "last visible result" means the actual result retained before the window ended, not a summary reconstructed later. If the original state has already been changed, record any new result separately; do not overwrite the earlier record.

## Exit action checks

1. [ ] First confirm that the dependency check has been performed. Having checked dependencies only means that the check left a record; it does not replace verification of the exit action itself.
2. [ ] Compare the hash at the exit entry point with the execution record. If they match, continue to retain the comparison result; if they differ, stop closing the window immediately. Do not use the old download entry point to fill the gap. That download entry point has been disabled and can no longer be used for recovery or verification.
3. [ ] Check whether the exit action has an explicit stop condition. If there is no stop condition, keep the window open and simply record the missing item; do not infer that rollback is complete because "there are no more new downloads."
4. [ ] Do not clear the original execution record, entry-point description, or last result until the exit action can be matched to the record. If the material needs to be condensed, retain the originals and explanations, not just a one-line summary conclusion.

A mismatch between the exit entry point and the execution record does not automatically mean either one is wrong. The current checklist does not have enough material to determine which step produced the difference; that state is itself a stop condition. If a new entry point or execution record becomes available later, a new record should be added rather than rewriting this comparison.

## Handoff before closing the window

- [ ] Record unfinished items separately under "exit action," "missing record sequence," and "mismatch between entry point and execution record." Do not merge them into a generic release risk.
- [ ] When someone takes over the action at hand, hand off only what still needs checking for this window; retain the fact that the long-term owner is unknown.
- [ ] Confirm that no one is still treating the disabled download entry point as a usable path for this exit.
- [ ] Pass the final visible result, entry-point discrepancies, and whether work stopped within the window to the person signing off on the release. That person can decide the release status, but their sign-off cannot restore intermediate events that are already missing.

Failure handling is simple: if the exit entry point and execution record do not match, the stop condition is not documented, or someone asks for missing intermediate records to be invented, stop closing this window. Do not execute rollback actions that have not been tried in the shared environment. If recovery is required, you can only start by preserving the state and opening a separate record; this page has no recovery command to copy and run as-is.

Related entry points: ERXD-003 record the limits of the temporary handoff for the action at hand; ERXD-006 flag the lack of a rollback command or stop condition for the exit action; ERXD-008 require that windows with no records be left blank. DOC-39 can be used to revisit the current entry point, but not as a substitute for this exit checklist.

# Decision Record for Public Entry Point Maintenance

This record preserves the trade-offs from the team's review of public entry point maintenance at the time. The discussion had a narrow focus: whether to keep the persistence-repository entry point or replace it during the change window. The meeting did not frame this as an opportunity for a comprehensive cleanup, nor did it assume that changing the entry point would automatically eliminate differences between callers.

The old draft described the approach as "keep it for now and revisit it later". That was enough to indicate a direction at the time, but it did not preserve what actually influenced the choice during the comparison. The added notes should keep that earlier position in its original time context: it reflected a working decision made before verification was complete, not a long-term rule that later maintainers could apply directly.

## Options Compared at the Meeting

Keeping the entry point did not mean doing nothing. This option required the entry point to remain accessible to callers while separating three aspects visible to them: how requests enter the boundary, the shape of the returned objects, and how state changes before and after the entry point. These three aspects cannot be summed up as "compatible", because a mismatch in any one of them would mix the effects of entry point changes with differences in the callers themselves in the same result.

The change option reversed the order: first change the entry point at the gem boundary, then have callers verify it at the new location. The benefit of this option was that legacy relationships would no longer consume maintenance attention, and the old entry point would not become a new long-term dependency. Its risk was not that the change would necessarily be wrong, but that there was not yet enough material to compare requests, returned objects, and state transitions individually. Once the entry point had changed, those performing verification could only work backward from the changed behavior to reconstruct the original state.

The meeting materials required a record of the actual impact, the coordinator, and the old entry point to roll back to. Here, "actual impact" did not mean listing every module that might be affected, but acknowledging what keeping the entry point would leave in place: legacy calls would still have a reference location, and the entry point's historical baggage would remain; immediate replacement might reduce maintenance costs, but it would also increase the risk of losing a reference for the original behavior. Both impacts were recognized in the choice made at the time, and neither was treated as nonexistent.

At the time, some people tended to treat the file location as the answer to who owned the entry point. Subsequent verification showed that this interpretation went too far. The location actually found was:

`elasticsearch-persistence/lib/elasticsearch/persistence/repository/search.rb`

Together with the related call names, it could provide a starting point for a local search, making it easier to return to the area around the entry point for further checks. The file location could show where verification began, but it could not, on its own, determine the long-term maintenance arrangements for the team's public entry point. The old draft did not spell out this distinction, so it had to be added later.

## Reasons for Keeping the Entry Point

An immediate switch was ultimately not approved in this round. The core of the decision was the order of work: first reproduce the requests, returned objects, and state transitions observed when calling Fang Ke, then determine the minimal compatibility changes at the gem boundary based on what had been reproduced. Here, "minimal" did not simply mean changing as few lines as possible, nor did it mean leaving the old entry point untouched for later; it meant limiting changes to behavior that could already be explained, without using the change as an opportunity to clean up legacy relationships that had not yet been accounted for.

Keeping the current entry point allowed verification to proceed against an unchanged reference. Requests could first be examined as the caller passed them into the boundary, returned objects could then be examined separately for the shape received by the caller, and state transitions could be checked last for discernible changes before and after the entry point. This order did not guarantee a complete answer every time, but it could prevent a single entry point replacement from changing all three categories of observations at once and leaving the causes to guesswork afterward.

The old entry point was called a "rollback location" because this decision needed to leave room to return to the original location. This was not an endorsement of the old entry point's value, nor did it mean that it had acquired permanent status. What was known at the time of the review was only this: while the comparison was still incomplete, removing the entry point would deprive later judgments of a reference; how long it should ultimately remain and who should maintain it on an ongoing basis were outside the scope of this decision.

The proposal to make the change directly was not judged to be wrong either. Its supporters were concerned that the continued existence of the old entry point would make legacy calls appear to remain encouraged, and that the maintenance burden would grow over time. This concern was valid, so the decision was not written as "never switch"; it was simply that long-term costs were not accepted at the time as a reason to skip reproduction. If sufficient comparisons became available later, the change window could still be discussed again.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Keep the current entry point] --> B[Reproduce requests]
  B --> C[Check returned objects]
  C --> D[Check state transitions]
  D --> E[Determine minimal changes at the gem boundary]
  E --> F[Keep a rollback location]
  G[Change the entry point immediately] -.Comparison was lacking at the time.-> B
```

The path in the diagram that starts with keeping the entry point was the work sequence approved at the time, not a migration process that had already been completed. The "immediate change" branch on the right was not permanently forbidden either; it was halted in that review because the comparisons needed before entering that branch had not yet been established.

## The Decision Did Not Expand the Scope

The review approved only what the existing evidence could cover. This limit applied to the three categories of observations: include requests in verification where they can be accounted for; include returned objects in verification where they can be accounted for; discuss entry point changes on that basis only where state transitions can be accounted for. If any one of the three is missing, do not use the other two as substitutes or record speculation as a confirmed compatibility relationship.

This round therefore did not approve rewriting the entry point in one pass while also cleaning up related naming, nor did it approve using a new abstraction to cover all the legacy relationships that had not yet been explained. These approaches might reduce the future maintenance burden, but they would expand the review's scope from observed behavior to areas unsupported by the available material. What the decision preserved was a narrow change window, not a comprehensive cleanup plan.

"Handle only minimal compatibility changes" had another meaning here: do not merge potentially different observations across callers into a single representative behavior. The way a request enters, the shape of a returned object, or a change in a state transition becomes a basis for modification only when it can be matched up during actual verification. The review did not authorize erasing these differences in advance merely because the entry point names were the same.

The coordinator was also listed as an item to record, but no individual's name was written on this page from memory at the time. The entry point maintainers need to confirm who will take over the handoff when the actual switch occurs; this is handled separately from the decision itself. The decision established the conditions under which the entry point could be changed, while confirming the coordinator establishes who will continue to follow up once those conditions are met. Mixing the two questions would instead make a draft without a name look as though it had reached no conclusion.

## Notes Added After Subsequent Verification

Subsequent verification still began around that file and the call names. It confirmed a findable entry point location, not a permanent ownership map. The earlier claim that "the file is here, so maintenance responsibility is here too" should be preserved as a simplified judgment from that time, but should no longer serve as a basis for this round's decision. Maintenance arrangements for the public entry point need to be confirmed during the handoff, and cannot be replaced by a single path lookup.

The added notes also revisited the three items in the old draft: "requests, returned objects, and state transitions". They are not different ways of describing the same check: requests concern what callers bring into the boundary; returned objects concern what callers get back; state transitions concern what changes occur before and after the entry point. The old draft merely listed the three together, and only later was it made explicit that each required its own supporting material. This correction did not overturn the decision to keep the entry point first; instead, it explained why switching first and verifying afterward could not be approved at the time.

One earlier assessment should not be edited away: the old entry point might be nothing more than historical baggage, or it might still be the only available reference for some callers. There was no material at the time to collapse those two possibilities into a single conclusion. Keeping the entry point was therefore a working choice made to control risk, not an assessment of its future value. Describing it as "all callers need the old entry point", or conversely as "the old entry point no longer has any value", would go beyond what this review actually knew.

Likewise, the fact that the change option was shelved at the time did not mean it could not be adopted later. It was shelved because of the order in which evidence was needed, not because the change itself was rejected. If comparable records of requests, returned objects, and state transitions are available, the next window can assess whether minimal changes are still all that is needed; if any one of them still lacks a corresponding record, continuing to keep the entry point is more consistent with the rationale preserved in this decision than changing first and guessing afterward.

## Items Left for the Switch Handoff

When the actual switch takes place, the coordinator, the rollback location for the old entry point, and the handoff actions need to be linked to DOC-44. The handoff steps are not expanded on here, to avoid treating "why we did not switch immediately at the time" and "how to hand things over when switching" as the same issue. DOC-44 became available as navigation material only after this page, so the initial draft did not cite it in advance.

The division of responsibilities between the two pages remains limited: this page preserves the two paths compared at the time, the approved sequence, and the reasons for not adopting the other option; the handoff material addresses what should be recorded during the actual switch. Later maintainers who only want to confirm whether the entry point can be changed immediately should return to the comparison conditions on this page; if the switch is already underway, they should then consult the location arrangements on the handoff page.

This decision can still explain why that review stopped at "reproduce first, change second". It does not confirm unwritten long-term ownership on behalf of later maintainers, nor does it elevate a single file lookup into a conclusion about team responsibility. The old entry point was kept so that known behavior would still have a reference; whether to change it, and how much to change, always depends on whether the three categories of observations can each be accounted for later.

# persistence-repository Entry Guide

`elasticsearch-persistence/lib/elasticsearch/persistence/repository/search.rb` remains the first stop for this review. After opening the file, first find the search entry exposed by the repository, then follow only one direct call relationship outward. This order is more reliable than guessing ownership from directory names: the file path tells you where to start reading, while the entry in the file tells you where the request leaves the repository boundary.

```text
persistence-repository
        |
        v
search.rb's public repository entry
        |
        v
A direct caller
        |
        v
The first real consumer under the team-wide public-entry owner
```

The previous version placed "file location" and "actual entry" too close together. That judgment is natural on a first read because the path is clear, and the filename also looks like the landing point for the search implementation. The distinction retained after review is that `search.rb` is the lookup starting point, not automatically the owner of the public entry. What must actually be confirmed is what entry it exposes and which direct caller that entry hands the request to. Only when the latter continues on to a real consumer does this local path take shape.

## Start inside the file

When reading the file, first note the name of the public repository entry and the object it hands off directly. There is no need to list the entire persistence directory or draw all dependencies. The only thing to trace is the call point through which the search request leaves the repository side. If the file contains several similar strings, choose one based on the actual call relationship. Content with only a name and no edge stays as a side note; do not treat it as the next hop.

Follow only one direct caller for the first hop. Once you reach that caller, continue from its existing entry until you reach the first real consumer under the team-wide public-entry owner. This stopping point serves two purposes: it distinguishes this page from a file index and a project overview, and it prevents subsequent internal implementation from being written up as entry ownership. Even if another caller can still be found, do not expand it alongside the first one; that would turn a single entry-location exercise into a consumer list.

If the direct caller exposes only request forwarding and does not show a consumer under the public-entry owner, stop at that caller and retain the relationship as unconfirmed. Do not use same-named methods, similar directories, or a one-line regression result to fill in a missing edge. This stopping point does not mean the call chain ends there; it means this page no longer has enough local relationships to name the next node.

## How to use the regression matrix

Use the multi-version regression matrix alongside entry tracing. First compare the version behavior in the matrix with the search entry being read to confirm that the call currently seen belongs to the same compatibility path; then return to the file to check the entry and the direct caller. The matrix can help distinguish how the same entry behaves across versions and indicate what type of phenomenon to trace back from during a review, but it cannot replace the call relationship in the file.

For example, when a test case name in the matrix appears together with `repository` in another path, do not merge the two records yet. Return to `search.rb` and check whether the repository entry actually hands off the request. If no call edge to the other file is visible, retain that file only as a signpost. Conversely, if the direct caller clearly hands the request to a public entry, follow that edge to confirm the first real consumer. The matrix is used here to cross-check entry behavior, not to infer maintenance responsibility from similar names.

## Handling same-named files

Same-named files create three common sources of confusion: nearby paths, identical filenames, and both containing `persistence` or `repository`. None of these similarities proves that they jointly maintain one entry. During a review, always restart from `elasticsearch-persistence/lib/elasticsearch/persistence/repository/search.rb`, first confirm its public entry, and then confirm the direct caller. A file not reached from this edge should not be written down as a subsequent node.

If a same-named file only provides a search-term hit, it can help with relocation, but it cannot replace the reading order on this page. If it is actually reached by the direct caller, continue confirming the relationship based on the object handed off by the caller; if only the directory name is similar, stop at the side note. This preserves the file's usefulness as a signpost without mistaking a search hit for an implementation chain.

## Boundary with the deviation record

This page keeps only the code-reading route from persistence-repository to the consumer under the public-entry owner. The symptom of a window deviation is documented separately in DOC-46; once DOC-46 is already in place, it can serve as a field clue for entering this page, but it cannot replace confirmation of the entry in the file. The two pages serve different purposes: the deviation record explains what happened in the window, while this page explains which file location to start from and which direct call edge to follow.

The final reading rule is: first treat `search.rb` as the starting point and find the public repository entry; then follow one direct caller; stop at the first real consumer. Directory locations, same-named files, and the regression matrix can only help with navigation; none can determine the maintenance relationship on its own. Stop where another owner needs to answer, and do not write speculation as ownership.

title: Public entry point maintenance deviation postmortem

versions.body:
# Public Entry Point Maintenance Discrepancy Postmortem

During the maintenance window, the results from the team's public entry point did not match the original plan. The first priority was not to explain the discrepancy, but to confirm whether the entry point could still be used and preserve the records of client calls already made as they stood at the time. There was not enough evidence on hand to attribute the anomaly to a specific change, so this record covers only observations during the window, the temporary recovery, and what remains unknown.

## Window Timeline

- After maintenance started, we monitored the public entry point as planned and saw results that did not match expectations. The initial anomaly was a deviation in entry point behavior, not a confirmed root cause.
- After spotting the discrepancy, we first checked the client call records and saved the entry point results observed at the time. The call records support reviewing requests that passed through the anomalous entry point; they cannot establish on their own which step caused the discrepancy.
- The priority then shifted to restoring entry point availability. To avoid propagating unconfirmed changes further, we retained the old entry point as a temporary recovery path that could be rolled back.
- After temporary recovery, the entry point was usable again. The window ended there, but the recovery only removed the immediate impact; it did not establish why the original plan had not produced the expected results.

## Impact Confirmed at the Time

The confirmed impact was limited to the public entry point during the maintenance window: visible results differed from the original plan, and the relevant client calls need to be reviewed one by one against the retained records. The available material does not provide a complete count of affected calls or indicate that all callers experienced the same result. We therefore did not broaden the scope to data changes, persistent failures, or failure of all calls.

During the response, entry point status and the cause could easily be conflated. Restoring usability only showed that the temporary path worked; it did not mean the original plan had been carried out correctly. On the other hand, client call records can preserve where requests passed through, but are not enough to attribute the discrepancy to a stage outside the entry point. The two types of information are kept separately to prevent the post-recovery state from overwriting the anomaly observed during maintenance.

## Recovery Record

The old entry point was retained as a reversible path so the public entry point could be made usable again first, while leaving room to switch back again and compare. Here, "old" refers only to the entry point used for recovery at the time; it does not mean it had been established as a long-term solution. When the window ended, temporary recovery was not recorded as a final fix, nor was the investigation into the cause closed on that basis.

When organizing the material from the response, we added three control points: actual impact needs to be documented based on the call records already retained; the coordinator needs to be identified during the window; the old entry point used for recovery must be reversible. These are intended to avoid being left with only the post-recovery results next time; they do not supply a root cause for this discrepancy.

## Still Unconfirmed

We still need to check where the original plan and actual results first diverged, which client calls actually passed through the anomalous entry point, and whether similar discrepancies were present after temporary recovery. This record does not reach a final conclusion on the cause. If more material is added later, retain both the entry point results observed during the anomaly and the call records from before and after recovery; keeping only the recovered state would obscure the discrepancy first observed during this window.

# Public Entry Point Result Discrepancy Troubleshooting Tree

The ticket says complete, but the results can't be verified. Triage in this order:

```text
Results differ
├─ The call entry point or version for indexing-import isn't clearly documented
│  └─ Add the missing records; stop if you can't.
├─ The same input produces different results across versions
│  └─ Add it to the multi-version regression matrix.
└─ Results still differ with the same input, entry point, and version
   └─ Record the actual impact and contact the coordinator; stop if the maintainer needs to change.
```

Don't remove the old entry point yet. The number of reruns is no substitute for entry point and version records.

```text
Results differ
├─ Entry point unclear, or version missing
│  └─ Add the missing records; if you still can't, stop at the ticket without assigning it further.
├─ Entry point known; results differ across versions for the same input
│  └─ Add it to the multi-version regression matrix, noting the differences and actual impact.
└─ Results still differ with the same input, entry point, and version
   └─ Take these records to the coordinator; if a new owner is needed, the tree ends here.
```

If the matrix is missing columns, add them; don't use the output in front of you as historical results. Don't remove the old entry point just because a discrepancy appears, either; act only after the coordinator confirms it can be withdrawn. If the scope of impact is unclear, mark it "unconfirmed" first. Repeated reruns are no substitute for this triage.
